name: Hydrolyzed silk protein

lead: Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk split into smaller peptides and amino acids, found in conditioners and cleansers. People use it for softer, smoother, shinier-looking hair.

Silk is mostly fibroin with a coating of sericin, and the small fragments are meant to coat the strands. It appears in patents for washing gels and permanent-wave compositions; no human study of hair appearance was found.

paras: It is used as an ingredient in conditioners, masks and cleansers, with the effect noticeable after each wash.
No hair-specific safety data were found in the sources reviewed.

angle.text: Hydrolyzed silk protein is added to conditioners so small silk peptides coat the strands, leaving hair softer, smoother and glossier after use. Hair trials of the ingredient were not found.

lead: Hydrolyzed silk protein is silk protein broken into smaller peptides and amino acids, used in cosmetic products including hair conditioners. Silk is mainly fibroin with a coating of sericin.[1]
Cosmetic formulations containing it appear in patents for washing gels and permanent-wave compositions.[2][3] No clinical trial found tests it for hair appearance.

paras: Silk is about 75-80 percent fibroin with a glue-like sericin coating, though proportions vary by source.[1] Hydrolysis yields shorter protein fragments.

Patent documents list hydrolyzed silk protein as an ingredient in a bath foam-cream and a washing gel.[2][3] A 1989 permanent-waving patent combined hydrogen-bonding amino acids with a silicone compound to claim improved curl retention and hair feel.[4]
A 2010 study in diabetic mice examined silk protein hydrolysates for blood glucose and lipids.[5] It does not concern hair.
No studies found for hair use.
